m3-t1.introduction: Choose a delivery approach for the uncertainty you face, not for its label. The visuals separate fixed controls from adaptable design and make each feedback loop produce evidence.

sections.section: 1. Agile values are trade-offs, not bans
sections.title: “More valuable” is not “the other side is worthless”
sections.explanation: Agile values guide a trade-off when priorities compete. A useful plan, agreement or document can still support collaboration and continuity. Ask what helps the team learn and deliver here rather than eliminating documentation to appear Agile.

items.label: People and working outcomes
items.detail: Interactions, collaboration and inspectable work help reveal needs.

items.label: Plans and supporting records
items.detail: Enough documentation, tools and agreements to make decisions durable.

items.label: Respond with evidence
items.detail: Change an approach when feedback warrants it, while respecting constraints.

sections.caption: Conceptual reading aid for the Agile values, not a replacement for the complete Manifesto or a ban on plans and contracts.
sections.takeaway: Avoid turning a relative preference into an absolute prohibition.

sections.title: Match the approach to what can still change
sections.explanation: Stable requirements can justify a predictive plan; uncertain workflows benefit from early trials. The same pilot can keep privacy and procurement controls fixed while iterating on booking design. This is a reasoned hybrid, not a claim that all activities are Scrum.

items.label: Predictive where stable
items.detail: Plan well-understood work with agreed acceptance and dependencies.

items.label: Adaptive where uncertain
items.detail: Test a small usable workflow and let feedback change the next slice.

items.label: Hybrid across boundaries
items.detail: Retain necessary approvals while adapting the solution design.

sections.caption: Illustrative approach choices for the fictional pilot. A fixed date does not remove uncertainty or authorise bypassing controls.
sections.takeaway: Explain which uncertainty the chosen method helps manage.

sections.title: A useful iteration changes a decision
sections.explanation: Set a learning question, expose something real enough to inspect and record what the observation can and cannot support. A tiny trial can reveal usability problems without proving a universal winner. Keep the event date and privacy boundary visible while adapting the next work.

items.label: Frame the question
items.detail: Which booking flow can volunteers complete unaided?

items.label: Test a small slice
items.detail: Observe the same defined journeys, not only a slide deck.

items.label: Inspect the evidence
items.detail: Flow A: 6/8; Flow B: 7/8, with limitations.

items.label: Adapt the next work
items.detail: Investigate failures and update the ordered backlog.

sections.caption: Synthetic lesson trial with eight volunteers. The small difference is a learning prompt, not statistically proven superiority.
sections.takeaway: Feedback without a recorded decision is not a complete learning loop.

checkpoint.question: Does seven out of eight prove Flow B is the best design for everyone?
checkpoint.answer: No. It is a small synthetic volunteer trial. Use the observations to plan further checks while preserving the fixed privacy and event constraints.

m3-t2.introduction: Connect Scrum accountabilities, events and commitments without turning them into a command hierarchy. An honest Increment must meet Done even when an optional item is removed.

sections.section: 1. Three accountabilities, not a command chain
sections.title: Three accountabilities share a product focus
sections.explanation: Each accountability serves a different purpose. The Product Owner orders value, Developers manage how to create the usable Increment, and the Scrum Master helps establish Scrum and improve effectiveness. A sponsor assigning every daily task would undermine that self-management.

items.label: Product Owner
items.detail: Accountable for product value and effective Product Backlog management.

items.label: Developers
items.detail: Create the usable Increment and adapt their own plan.

items.label: Scrum Master
items.detail: Establish Scrum and support team effectiveness; not a task dispatcher.

sections.caption: Conceptual accountability map. It is not an organisational reporting line or a claim of external Scrum certification.
sections.takeaway: Accountability does not make one role the boss of every decision.

sections.section: 2. Events create opportunities to inspect and adapt
sections.title: Inspect the product and improve the way of working
sections.explanation: The Sprint contains the other events. Planning creates focus, the Daily Scrum helps Developers adapt their plan, the Review inspects outcomes with stakeholders, and the Retrospective improves quality and effectiveness. Refinement continues as needed; it is not an extra official event.

items.label: Sprint Planning
items.detail: Establish a Sprint Goal and a plan for valuable work.

items.label: Daily Scrum
items.detail: Developers inspect progress and adapt in 15 minutes.

items.label: Sprint Review
items.detail: Inspect the outcome with stakeholders and adapt future work.

items.label: Sprint Retrospective
items.detail: Choose improvements to quality and effectiveness.

sections.caption: Conceptual event map inside a Sprint of one month or less. The Review is not a mandatory release gate; the loop is not drawn to time scale.
sections.takeaway: Name an event by its purpose, not merely by how often a meeting happens.

sections.title: Pair each artefact with its commitment
sections.explanation: Commitments make the artefacts interpretable. A long backlog needs a Product Goal, a Sprint plan needs a Sprint Goal, and an Increment needs a shared Definition of Done. Moving an unsafe item into the Done column cannot replace the quality commitment.

items.label: Product Backlog ↔ Product Goal
items.detail: The longer-term objective gives ordered work direction.

items.label: Sprint Backlog ↔ Sprint Goal
items.detail: The objective focuses the Developers’ adaptable plan.

items.label: Increment ↔ Definition of Done
items.detail: The usable result meets shared quality expectations.

sections.caption: Conceptual Scrum artefact/commitment pairings. Item acceptance criteria and release decisions remain related but distinct.
sections.takeaway: Scope can be renegotiated without declaring an unsafe item Done.

checkpoint.question: Can a team remove an optional reminder while keeping unsafe booking work out of the Increment?
checkpoint.answer: Yes. It can renegotiate scope with the Product Owner while protecting the Sprint Goal. Work failing the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment.

m3-t3.introduction: Move from a large feature label to small usable slices, then forecast within actual focused capacity. Story points are not silently converted into hours.

sections.section: 1. A story is a conversation starter
sections.title: A story needs examples, not only a sentence
sections.explanation: The story format opens a conversation about a user, a need and a reason. Item-specific examples then describe how success and failure should behave. Shared Done adds the quality expectations that apply to all items; it is not a substitute for the item’s examples.

items.label: User, need and reason
items.detail: A learner wants to cancel so the slot becomes available.

items.label: Item acceptance examples
items.detail: Valid cancellation, invalid reference and repeated cancellation.

items.label: Shared Definition of Done
items.detail: Required tests, reviews and usable quality apply across items.

sections.caption: Illustrative cancellation story. Technical tasks need not be forced into invented user personas.
sections.takeaway: A correct story template does not prove the work is understood.

sections.section: 2. Slice by value rather than only layers
sections.title: Slice a journey, not just a technology layer
sections.explanation: A thin usable journey crosses the layers needed for one meaningful outcome. Database-only, interface-only and report-only items can be useful tasks, but they may leave nothing a user can inspect until all are finished. Reduce breadth without dropping the quality needed for safe use.

items.label: Thin booking slice
items.detail: A small end-to-end path lets a learner reserve safely.

items.label: Next value slice
items.detail: Cancellation can be inspected as its own usable outcome.

items.label: Supporting technical tasks
items.detail: Data, interface and integration tasks support the slice; they are not each user value.

sections.caption: Conceptual slicing comparison for the pilot. Ordering still considers risk, dependencies and learning as well as value.
sections.takeaway: The Product Owner orders work; the slice still has to meet Done.

sections.section: 3. Forecast with capacity and past evidence
sections.title: Forecast from available people-days, not nominal seats
sections.explanation: Three members for ten days would be thirty person-days, but two absent days reduce this to twenty-eight. Five focused hours per available day produces 140 hours before other commitments. This is the lesson fixture; the project block separately deducts ten support hours.

items.label: Nominal before absence
items.detail: 3 × 10 person-days × 5 hours = 150.

items.label: Lesson capacity after absence
items.detail: (30 − 2) × 5 = 140 before support deductions.

sections.caption: Synthetic lesson capacity, not the PB2 net forecast of 130 hours. These are alternative capacity states, not amounts to add; no story-point conversion is implied.
sections.takeaway: Make leave, support work and uncertainty visible before selecting work.

checkpoint.question: Should this lesson’s 140 hours be copied unchanged into PB2?
checkpoint.answer: No. PB2 adds a separate ten-hour support reservation: 140 − 10 = 130 focused hours. Neither value defines a universal hours-per-point rule.

m3-pb2.introduction: Make the Sprint simulation goal-driven, capacity-aware and honest about unfinished work. The net 130-hour capacity is specific to this project block, not a conversion from story points.

sections.title: Simulate a goal, not a board full of activity
sections.explanation: Booking and cancellation are needed; reminders are optional. Connect the Product Goal to a Sprint Goal and a small usable slice, then make the defect/change response preserve quality. Represent the work as a classroom simulation, not live software delivery.

items.label: Product direction
items.detail: Describe the valuable booking/cancellation outcome.

items.label: Ordered backlog
items.detail: Use value, risk, dependencies and learning to explain order.

items.label: Sprint forecast
items.detail: Select a coherent slice within actual focused capacity.

items.label: Inspectable result
items.detail: Meet Done or keep the item unfinished; record the adaptation.

sections.caption: Conceptual PB2 delivery simulation. No real Scrum team, release or customer outcome is implied.
sections.takeaway: An optional item can leave the forecast; mandatory Done cannot.

sections.title: Use the project’s net capacity, not a copied lesson total
sections.explanation: The three-person team loses two person-days to absence. The project then reserves ten focused hours for support. Keep those deductions visible so the Sprint selection is not based on nominal availability. A sandbox, spreadsheet or paper board can all hold the evidence.

items.label: Available person-days
items.detail: 3 × 10 − 2 = 28 before other commitments.

items.label: Focused capacity
items.detail: 28 × 5 = 140 hours before the support reservation.

items.label: PB2 net capacity
items.detail: 140 − 10 support hours = 130 focused hours.

sections.caption: Synthetic PB2 inputs. The lesson’s 140-hour example has not yet deducted these support hours; no fixed story-points-to-hours rule is created.
sections.takeaway: Label the scope and period of every capacity number.

sections.title: PB2: reserve time to verify and revise
sections.explanation: The classroom block is not all build time. Use the reproduction checkpoint to trace the headline result to source values, then retain the peer comment and correction. The final recommendation should follow the revised evidence, not the first attractive draft.

items.label: Frame and inspect
items.detail: Read the brief, boundaries and source fixtures.

items.label: Build required artefacts
items.detail: Create the linked outputs for this block.

items.label: Reproduce and review
items.detail: Check calculations, definitions and decisions.

items.label: Peer review and revise
items.detail: Keep the comment and the response.

items.label: Recommendation and AI statement
items.detail: Explain the decision and assistance transparently.

sections.caption: Published synthetic classroom allocation for PB2: 20 + 80 + 35 + 30 + 15 = 180 minutes. This is learner work time, not the delivery schedule’s working days.
sections.takeaway: A checked second version is more valuable than an unchecked first draft.

sections.title: Connect commitments, slice and feedback evidence
sections.explanation: A marker should be able to follow why the selected items support the goal, how they will be accepted and what changed when a defect appeared. Use the event map to explain purpose rather than inventing a required ceremony for every activity.

items.label: Goals and backlog
items.detail: Product Goal, Sprint Goal, six ordered items and reasons.

items.label: Examples and Done
items.detail: Item examples for three items plus shared quality expectations.

items.label: Capacity and slice
items.detail: Worksheet, forecast selection and a small end-to-end outcome.

items.label: Event purposes
items.detail: Planning, Daily Scrum, Review and Retrospective distinguished.

items.label: Adaptation and learning
items.detail: Simulated defect/change, updated scope and improvement action.

sections.caption: Conceptual map of PB2’s published submissions. External files and facilitator marking remain separate from platform reading and quizzes.
sections.takeaway: A board screenshot alone cannot explain the forecast or Done.

sections.title: 130 hours is a forecast input, not a guarantee
sections.explanation: The capacity states below are alternatives in a deduction sequence, not quantities to sum. Select a useful goal and preserve uncertainty even after the arithmetic is right. If an item fails Done, the honest result is unfinished work rather than a convenient column change.

items.label: Nominal before absence
items.detail: 30 person-days × 5 hours = 150.

items.label: After absence
items.detail: 28 person-days × 5 hours = 140.

items.label: After support reservation
items.detail: 140 − 10 = 130 available for the PB2 forecast.

sections.caption: Synthetic PB2 capacity waterfall shown as zero-based comparison bars. These are successive states, not additive work or story-point conversions.
sections.takeaway: Capacity constrains a forecast; it does not justify cutting quality.

checkpoint.question: What remains after absence and the PB2 support reservation?
checkpoint.answer: (3 × 10 − 2) × 5 − 10 = 130 focused hours. A selected item still must meet Done to become part of the usable Increment.

sections.title: Seven marks reward evidence and judgement
sections.explanation: Use the published rubric to inspect the work, not to invent new requirements. Correct arithmetic needs traceable inputs, professional judgement includes safeguards and authority, and clarity includes an evidence trail and reflection. The diagram does not award or upload marks.

items.label: Correctness and reproducibility
items.detail: Show the method, source values and a manual check.

items.label: Judgement and safeguards
items.detail: Make limits, provenance, authority and safe sharing explicit.

items.label: Clarity, evidence and reflection
items.detail: Keep the files navigable and explain the correction.

sections.caption: Illustrative display of the unchanged PB2 rubric: 3 + 2 + 2 = 7. Four blocks contribute 28 overall; external facilitator marking remains required.
sections.takeaway: Appearance alone cannot earn credit for an unsupported claim.

sections.title: Review the coherence of the Sprint story
sections.explanation: Ask a peer to find the goal, recalculate capacity and trace one changed item. If the story claims a usable result, its criteria and Done evidence must support that claim. Keep the limitation or correction instead of editing history into a flawless Sprint.

items.label: Goal alignment
items.detail: Do the selected items support the stated Sprint Goal?

items.label: Capacity check
items.detail: Can the reviewer reproduce 130 without mixing units?

items.label: Quality check
items.detail: Which item is unfinished and why?

items.label: Adaptation check
items.detail: What evidence changed scope or the improvement action?

sections.caption: Conceptual project peer-review aid; this is not a substitute for, or a renaming of, the Scrum Sprint Review event.
sections.takeaway: Correct framework terms should explain the evidence, not decorate it.

sections.title: Disclose assistance and keep responsibility
sections.explanation: For the Sprint simulation, assistance can support drafting or checking, but it cannot create evidence that never existed. Complete the statement even if the answer is “none”. Keep only synthetic inputs in public tools and make your own verification visible.

items.label: Disclose use
items.detail: Tool or none, task assisted, and synthetic inputs shared.

items.label: Record your choices
items.detail: Suggestions accepted, changed or rejected, with your own contribution.

items.label: Verify independently
items.detail: Recompute net capacity, verify Scrum commitments and distinguish proposed acceptance from evidence that actually meets Done.

items.label: Respect assessment boundaries
items.detail: Do not infer final-exam permission from project-tool permission.

sections.caption: Conceptual project AI-use workflow. It does not fabricate approvals, interviews, sources, business results or personal experience.
sections.takeaway: The learner remains responsible for the final numbers, claims and safeguards.

sections.title: Fixed approvals and adaptive design can coexist
sections.explanation: The optional extension is about choosing controls deliberately. Procurement and privacy approvals can remain predictive while the workflow design uses short feedback cycles. Explain the boundary rather than calling every meeting or activity Scrum.

items.label: Predictive control lane
items.detail: Required authorisations, event constraints and procurement milestones.

items.label: Adaptive learning lane
items.detail: Small usable workflow slices, inspected feedback and updated ordering.

items.label: Shared boundary
items.detail: No adaptive label permits bypassing safety, privacy or real authority.

sections.caption: Conceptual optional hybrid explanation. It is not required for full marks or a claim that any hybrid automatically follows Scrum.
sections.takeaway: Describe what stays fixed and what the evidence is allowed to change.
